questions.solution: The inequality x > -3 represents all real numbers greater than -3. In interval notation, this is written as (3, ∞).
questions.explanation: Interval notation uses parentheses to indicate that the endpoint is not included and square brackets to indicate that it is included. Since x can be any number greater than -3 but not equal to -3, we use an open parenthesis.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (A) because students may forget that the inequality sign points to the larger set and thus includes all values greater than -3.

questions.solution: The inequality y ≤ 7 represents all real numbers less than or equal to 7. In interval notation, this is written as (-∞, 7].
questions.explanation: Since the inequality includes values up to and including 7, we use a square bracket on the left side of the interval. The right side remains open because y can be any number less than 7.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (A) because students may confuse ≤ with > and forget that the endpoint is included.

questions.solution: The inequality -5 < z < 2 represents all real numbers between -5 and 2 (exclusive). In interval notation, this is written as (-5, 2).
questions.explanation: Both endpoints are excluded because the inequality uses '<' instead of ≤ or ≥. Therefore, we use open parentheses for both ends of the interval.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (B) because students may interpret the double inequality as inclusive endpoints.

questions.stem: Solve for w: w ≥ 0 and w < 10
questions.solution: The compound inequality w ≥ 0 and w < 10 represents all real numbers greater than or equal to 0 and less than 10. In interval notation, this is written as [0, 10).
questions.explanation: The first inequality includes 0, so we use a square bracket on the left side. The second inequality does not include 10, so we use an open parenthesis on the right side.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (A) because students may forget to consider the upper bound of the interval.

questions.stem: Solve for x: x < -4 or x ≥ 6
questions.solution: The compound inequality x < -4 or x ≥ 6 represents all real numbers less than -4 and greater than or equal to 6. In interval notation, this is written as (-∞, -4) ∪ (6, ∞).
questions.explanation: Both intervals are exclusive, so we use open parentheses for both ends. The first interval includes values less than -4, and the second interval includes values greater than 6.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (A) because students may interpret 'or' as inclusive endpoints.

questions.solution: The inequality -2 ≤ y ≤ 3 represents all real numbers between -2 and 3 (inclusive). In interval notation, this is written as [-2, 3].
questions.explanation: Both endpoints are included because the inequality uses '≤' for both sides. Therefore, we use square brackets for both ends of the interval.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (A) because students may forget to include the endpoint -2.

questions.stem: Solve for z: 4 ≤ z < 8 and z ≠ 6
questions.solution: The compound inequality 4 ≤ z < 8 and z ≠ 6 represents all real numbers greater than or equal to 4, less than 8, and not equal to 6. In interval notation, this is written as [4, 6) ∪ (6, 8].
questions.explanation: The first inequality includes 4, so we use a square bracket on the left side of the first interval. The second inequality excludes 6, so we exclude it from both intervals using open parentheses. The second interval continues to 8 but does not include it.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Common mistake: Choosing (B) because students may forget that z ≠ 6 means 6 is not included in the solution.
